Wilfully
WIL-ful-ee
adv. (by deliberate choice; of set purpose)
Greek hekousios, willingly, voluntarily, of one's own accord — the opposite of what is done under compulsion or in ignorance. The English compounds will with -ful: full of one's own will.

Biblical Definition

For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins. The warning is among the most solemn in Scripture and it must be read for exactly what it says. Hekousios means voluntarily, of set purpose — and the old covenant background matters, since the law made provision by sacrifice for sins of ignorance and made none for the sin of a high hand. The writer is not describing a believer who falls, repents, and is restored; David murdered and was forgiven, Peter denied and was restored. He is describing deliberate, settled, high-handed apostasy by a man who had received the knowledge of the truth and trampled it. The description he gives leaves no room for a lesser reading: he hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace. The reason no sacrifice remains is not that God's mercy has run short but that there is no other sacrifice; a man who has finally repudiated the one offering has nowhere left to go. What follows is meant to be felt: a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation; and, it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. The writer's own conclusion about his readers is nevertheless confident: we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): by design; with set purpose; obstinately; stubbornly.

expand to see more

WILFULLY, adv. By design; with set purpose or intention.

WILFUL, a. Governed by the will without yielding to reason; obstinate; stubborn; perverse.

WILFUL, a. Intentional; premeditated; as wilful murder.

PRESUMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; done with bold design or with contempt of divine law.

APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 10:26 — "For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins,"

Hebrews 10:27 — "But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries."

Hebrews 10:29 — "Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?"

Hebrews 10:31 — "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God."

Modern Corruption

The passage is used either to torment believers who have sinned seriously or to prove that a true Christian may finally perish; it describes high-handed apostasy and is given as a warning God uses to keep his own.

expand to see more

The pastoral damage done by misreading Hebrews 10:26 is considerable. Believers who have fallen badly conclude that they have committed the sin for which no sacrifice remains, and despair. The text does not describe them. It describes a man who has trodden the Son of God under foot, counted the blood of the covenant an unholy thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace — a settled and contemptuous repudiation, not a fall. The surest evidence that a person has not done this is that he fears he has; the man in view here is precisely the man who has stopped caring. A conscience still alive to the offence is the Spirit's work, not the absence of it.

Doctrinally the passage is pressed to overturn the perseverance of the saints. The Reformed answer does not soften the warning; it reads it alongside the same book's assurance and the Lord's own words that his sheep shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of his hand. Those who finally fall away were never truly his — they went out from us, but they were not of us. And the warning is not thereby made idle. God preserves his people through means, and this passage is one of them: a real danger, solemnly stated, which the Spirit uses to keep believers from the road that leads there. The writer applies it that way himself, and then tells his readers he is persuaded of better things concerning them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hekousios (G1596), willingly, of set purpose; epignosis (G1922), full knowledge; katapateo (G2662), to tread under foot; enubrizo (G1796), to insult or do despite to.

expand to see more

Greek hekousios (G1596) — voluntarily, of one's own will; rendered wilfully, its only occurrence.

Greek epignosis (G1922) — full or precise knowledge; what the apostate had received.

Greek katapateo (G2662) — to trample underfoot; rendered trodden under foot the Son of God.

Greek enubrizo (G1796) — to insult, to treat with contempt; rendered done despite unto the Spirit of grace.

Hebrew yad ramah (H3027, H7411) — a high hand; the old covenant category for which no sacrifice was provided.

Usage

"“if we sin wilfully” — of set purpose, not a fall."

"“counted the blood of the covenant… an unholy thing” — the man described."

"“we are not of them who draw back” — the writer's conclusion about his readers."
